newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: FOCUS-Brazil trading partners concerned about cars.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Brazil trading partners concerned about cars.

text.p: Brazil's trading partners expressed concern on Thursday over measures limiting access to the country's automotive and textile markets, officials said.

Brazil defended its trading regime and its new automobile tariff quota system, which covers only vehicles imported from Japan, South Korea and the European Union, saying it should greatly enhance access to its domestic market, they added.

The debate took place during a review of a report by the World Trade Organisation (WTO) which urged Sao Paulo to give a "more measured response" to pressure from some domestic sectors for protection from imports.
WTO said the automotive industry was the most highly-assisted manufacturing activity in Brazil, with effective protection estimated at more than 250 per cent.
"It was a mixed review, really," Anne Anderson, Irish ambassador, told a news briefing at the end of two-day, closed-door talks. Anderson also chairs the WTO trade policy review body.
"The high level of protection in the automotive sector was particularly commented on...Members sought information on the tariff quota system for vehicles recently introduced by Brazil."
In August, Brazil offered Japan, South Korea and EU members a combined annual quota of 50,000 vehicles, based on an average of their exports to Brazil from January 1993-April 1996.
Celso Lafer, Brazil's trade ambassador, said in a separate briefing "We have squarely tackled this concern through the tariff quota system."
Regarding the WTO estimate that Brazil's effective protection was more than 250 percent, he said "We would certainly like to have an idea of how they estimated this."
Jose Alfredo Graca Lima, head of Brazil's Foreign Ministry economics department, told the briefing "The decision to impose a tariff quota was a success.
"We are ready to listen to the United States to see whether any solution can be found to the problem they have indicated," he added.
The United States, not included in the tariff quota system, on October 1 launched a probe into Brazil's automotive regime under Section 301 of its controversial trade law.
Under U.S. law, this would allow Washington to retaliate after 90 days of bilateral consultations and investigation of charges of unfair trade practices brought by U.S. manufacturers.

Brazil has held bilateral consultations, the first step in the WTO dispute settlement procedure, with Japan, the United States, the European Union and South Korea who allege Brazil's car industry rules discriminate against imports.
No formal WTO dispute panel has been created yet to arbitrate in the automotive row.

Brazil is a large net exporter of vehicles and its motor industry achieved record production levels in 1995, according to the WTO report. Tariffs on motor vehicles increased to 70 percent in March 1995 from 20 percent in 1994.
"Under the automotive regime introduced in mid-1995, the industry benefits from tariff exemptions, combined with local-content and export balancing requirements," WTO said.

Regarding testiles, Anderson said some members expressed understanding for difficulties faced by the Brazilian textile industry, but some members believed the safeguard measures on textile products were not compatible with WTO provisions. Hong Kong and South Korea, both big producers, raised the issue.

Despite praise for Brazil's economic stabilisation, trade liberalisation and a more open investment regime, WTO members voiced concern over the gaps between tariff bindings and applied rates, relatively frequent resort to anti-dumping actions and continuing restrictions in the services sector, Anderson said.
"They strongly encouraged perseverance with the macroeconomic reform programme, resistance to protectionist pressures and strict adherence to WTO rules and procedures."
